title: Choosing the Right Atoms for GPU Kernel Development with CuTe DSL
critical_patterns: For MMA atoms, choose based on GPU architecture and precision needs.
Use cp.async for Ampere, TMA for Hopper, and TMA with TMEM for Blackwell for copy operations.
FP16 with FP32 accumulator is standard for training; FP8 is optimal for inference on Hopper and Blackwell.
BF16 is preferred for large models due to better range and similar speed to FP16.
constraints: Ensure architecture-specific atoms are used for optimal performance.
FP32 accumulators are recommended for long accumulation chains.
Validation is crucial to ensure accuracy and performance meet requirements.
Use lower precision only when accuracy loss is acceptable.
compressed_summary: This document provides guidance on selecting the appropriate atoms for GPU kernel development using the CuTe DSL, focusing on different GPU architectures (Ampere, Hopper, Blackwell) and data types (FP16, BF16, FP8, etc.). Key factors in atom selection include the target GPU architecture, precision requirements, performance vs accuracy trade-offs, and memory bandwidth constraints. For MMA atoms, the choice depends on the GPU architecture and the precision needed, with FP16 inputs and FP32 accumulators being the industry standard for training due to their balance of speed and precision. For inference, FP8 is recommended on Hopper and Blackwell GPUs for its speed advantage, while FP6 and FP4 are options for extreme quantization on Blackwell. Copy operations should utilize cp.async on Ampere, TMA on Hopper, and TMA with TMEM on Blackwell for efficient data movement. The document emphasizes the importance of validating kernel performance and accuracy, providing a decision matrix and validation checklist to guide users. It also outlines architecture-specific recommendations and common scenarios, such as LLM training and inference, vision model training, and quantized inference, offering practical examples and best practices for each case. The document concludes with a summary of decision factors and golden rules for atom selection, highlighting the importance of balancing speed and accuracy while ensuring thorough validation.
